_doc: Posting queue. status: building -> needs-voice -> ready -> sent. At each slot (11:45 + 18:45 ET) the oldest 'ready' item per channel is sent to the user with its caption, then marked 'sent'. No ready item = slot skipped, never filler. Final mp4s live in posting/ready/ (committed: they carry paid voice).

items.title: The 1% fee that eats 24% of your retirement
items.caption: 1% sounds like nothing. Over 40 years it quietly takes a quarter of your money. Here's the math.

items.title: A raise can't lower your pay (the tax bracket myth)
items.caption: Getting bumped into the 22% bracket doesn't put your whole paycheck at 22%. Only the dollars above the line. Here's the math on a $1,000 raise.

items.title: The minimum payment trap: $5,000, 19 years
items.caption: Pay only the minimum on a $5,000 card at 22% and it takes 19 years and $8,100 in interest. Keep paying that first payment instead and it's gone in under 5.

items.title: Lose 20%, gain 20%... you're still down
items.caption: $10,000 drops 20% to $8,000. A 20% gain only gets you to $9,600. You need 25% just to break even, and a 50% loss needs 100%.

items.title: The only instant 100% return (your 401k match)
items.caption: You put in $2,400, your employer adds $2,400. That's a 100% return on day one. Over 30 years, just the free half can grow to about $227K. Match terms and vesting vary.

items.title: When does your money double? Divide 72 by the rate
items.caption: At 8%, 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years to double. $10K becomes about $160K in 36 years. The same rule says a 24% credit card doubles your balance in about 3.

items.title: Your cash says $10,000. In 24 years it buys half.
items.caption: At 3% inflation, cash sitting at 0% loses half its buying power in about 24 years (72 ÷ 3). The number never changes. What it buys does.

items.title: The lower car payment that costs $3,124 more
items.caption: $40,000 car at 7% (example). 4 years: $958/mo, $5,977 interest. 6 years: $682/mo, $9,101 interest. 7 years: over $10,700. A smaller payment isn't a cheaper car.

items.title: "No interest for 12 months" — miss by $1, pay $195
items.caption: $1,200 TV on a store card, 0% if paid in full in 12 months. Leave $1 and you can owe ~$195 of interest on the full amount, back to day one. Look for the word "deferred." (Example at 29.99% APR; terms vary.)

items.title: A $1 billion jackpot isn't $1 billion
items.caption: The advertised jackpot is 30 payments over 29 years, each 5% bigger than the last. Take the cash today and it's under half: about $450M on a ~$1B jackpot, before taxes.

items.title: A $400K mortgage costs $910K
items.caption: 30 years at 6.5% (example): $2,528/mo, and $510K of it is interest. More than the house. Add $200/mo to principal and you finish 5.6 years early and keep ~$112K.

items.title: How much do you need to retire? Multiply by 25
items.caption: The 4% rule in one line: yearly spending × 25. Spend $40K a year, you need about $1M. Flip it: every $1/yr you cut is $25 less to save. Cut $100/month = $30,000 less. (Rule of thumb from historical data, not a guarantee.)

items.title: Switching doors doubles your odds (it feels wrong)
items.caption: Three doors, one car. Switching wins 2 out of 3 times. Your gut says 50/50. Your gut is wrong.

items.title: Africa is 14x bigger than Greenland. Your map lied.
items.caption: On the map on your wall they look the same size. They are not even close.

items.title: Astronauts aren't weightless. They're falling.
items.caption: Gravity on the space station is about 90% of what you feel right now. So why do they float?

items.title: Multiply any number by 11 in your head
items.caption: No calculator, two seconds. Pause and try 72 x 11 first.

items.title: 23 people, 50% chance two share a birthday
items.caption: 365 days, only 23 people, and it's a coin flip. The trick: it's not 23 chances, it's 253 pairs. At 70 people it's 99.9%.

items.title: A million seconds is 11 days. A billion is 31 years.
items.caption: One letter apart, so your brain files them side by side. A billion seconds ago was early 1995. A trillion seconds ago, people were painting cave walls.

items.title: Buses every 10 minutes. Why do you wait 10, not 5?
items.caption: Long gaps catch more riders because they're long. Here 78% of riders land in the two long gaps, so the average wait is the full 10 minutes. Same reason classes feel bigger than the school says.

items.title: A 99% accurate test says you're sick. You're probably fine.
items.caption: Rare disease, 1 in 1,000. Test 1,000 people: 1 real positive, about 10 false alarms. So a positive means about a 9% chance. Test positive twice and it jumps to 91%. (Illustration, not medical advice.)

items.title: Your friends have more friends than you (it's math)
items.caption: In this friend group, 7 of 8 people have fewer friends than their friends do. Popular people show up on everyone's list, so they get counted again and again. Scientists use it to spot flu outbreaks up to 2 weeks early.

items.title: 0.999... = 1. Not almost. Exactly.
items.caption: 1/3 = 0.333... Multiply by 3: 3/3 = 0.999... and 3/3 is 1. Still not sure? Try to find a number between them. There isn't one.

items.title: Wins both groups. Loses overall. (Real data)
items.caption: Kidney stone study: treatment A beat B for small stones (93% vs 87%) and large stones (73% vs 69%), but lost overall (78% vs 83%). A got the hard cases. That's Simpson's paradox.

items.title: 30% of real-world numbers start with a 1
items.caption: You'd expect each first digit 11% of the time. Take the first 1,000 powers of two: 301 start with a 1, only 45 with a 9. That's Benford's law, and auditors use it to catch made-up numbers.

items.title: The doctor who tried to cheat Death
items.caption: A Brothers Grimm tale: Death becomes a boy's godfather and gives him one gift. If Death stands at the head of the bed, the patient lives. At the feet, they die. Then the princess falls ill...

items.title: Pay in 4 is 0% interest. Miss one: ~730% APR
items.caption: Pay in 4 really is 0% interest... if you never miss. A $7 late fee on a $25 payment is 28% in two weeks, which works out to about 730% APR. The same $25 on a 22% credit card for two weeks costs about 21 cents. (Fees vary by lender and state; illustrative math, not advice.)

items.title: Three wishes. The third one knocked at the door.
items.caption: The Monkey's Paw (W. W. Jacobs, 1902). A cursed paw grants three wishes to prove that fate punishes anyone who meddles with it. The first wish was for £200. The second wish... you'll see. What would you have done with the last one? 🕯️

items.title: You paid in full. Your credit score still dropped.
items.caption: Your card usually reports your balance on the statement date, not the due date. Spend $900 on a $1,000 limit and pay it off on time: the bureaus still see 90% utilization. Amounts owed are about 30% of a FICO score. Pay before the statement closes and they see $50 instead, which is 5%. Same card, same spending, different date. (Illustrative, not advice.)

items.title: One key. One locked room. A stain that won't wash away.
items.caption: Bluebeard (Charles Perrault, 1697). His new bride got every key to the castle, and one rule: never open the little room at the end of the hall. She lasted one day. 🕯️ What would you have done when he came home early?

items.title: Mortgage points only pay off after 5 years
items.caption: One mortgage point costs 1% of the loan: $3,000 on $300K. If it cuts your rate from 6.50% to 6.25%, you save $49 a month. $3,000 ÷ $49 = 61 months to break even. Sell or refinance before about 5 years and the point lost you money. (Rate cut per point varies by lender; illustrative, not advice.)

items.title: Your car lease hides its interest rate. Multiply by 2400.
items.caption: Leases list a 'money factor' instead of an APR. Multiply it by 2,400 to translate: 0.00375 = 9% APR. On a $35K lease that's about $210 a month just in interest. The money factor is negotiable: get it to 6% and you save about $2,520 over 3 years. (Excludes taxes & fees; illustrative, not advice.)

items.title: They owed me my pay. So I took their children.
items.caption: Hamelin, 1284, told by the Pied Piper himself. I cleared their rats. They laughed at my bill. So I came back while they sat in church... 🕯️ If you were me, what would you have played? (The real Grimm legend, not the kids' version.)

items.title: You're $400 short. The sign says $15 per $100.
items.caption: Rent's due Friday and you're $400 short. The payday loan fee is $60 for two weeks, which sounds like 15%. That's 15% every two weeks: about 390% APR. Roll it over 5 times and you've paid $300 and still owe the $400. CFPB research: almost 70% of borrowers take a second payday loan within a month. (Fees vary by state; not advice.)

items.title: I hid behind a barrel and watched what my bridegroom does to his brides.
items.caption: The Robber Bridegroom (Brothers Grimm, 1812), told by the bride. A bird in a cage warned me: turn back, young bride. I didn't. 🕯️ Footsteps at the door. What would you have done?

items.title: You invest 10 years and stop. Your friend invests 30. You win.
items.caption: You put $200/month in from 25 to 35, then never add another dollar ($24K total). Your friend starts at 35 and invests $200/month for 30 years ($72K total). At 65, you have about $281K; they have about $244K. Ten extra years of compounding beat three times the money. Keep going all 40 years: about $525K. (Assumes 7%/yr average; returns vary; not advice.)

items.title: I carried a skull home through the forest. By morning, my stepmother was ash.
items.caption: Vasilisa and Baba Yaga (Russian folk tale, Afanasyev), told by Vasilisa. Sent into the forest for fire, to the hut on chicken legs and the fence of skulls with glowing eyes. All I had was my mother's little doll. 🕯️ Impossible work, one night. What would you do?

items.title: Black Friday: 'Open our card, save 20%.' Do the math first.
items.caption: $600 TV, 20% off for opening the store card: you save $120 and put $480 on a card averaging ~30% APR (Bankrate). Pay $25 a month and it takes 27 months, with $182 in interest. Your discount cost you $62. It only wins if you pay it all off before the first bill. (Illustrative; APRs vary; not advice.)

items.title: Your $3,000 tax refund isn't a bonus. It's a 0% loan. From you.
items.caption: A $3,000 refund means you overpaid $250 every month, and got 0% interest for it. That $250/mo in a 4% savings account: about +$55. Against a 22% credit card balance: about $322 less interest. A big refund is a year-long, zero-interest loan you made. (Illustrative; withholding depends on your situation; not tax advice.)

items.title: I'm not mad. Listen how calmly I can tell you the whole story.
items.caption: The Tell-Tale Heart (Edgar Allan Poe, 1843), told by the one who did it. It was the eye. Pale blue, with a film over it. And then, under the floor... that sound. 🕯️ Where would you have hidden him? 🎧 Sound on.

items.title: The latte isn't why you're broke. Here's the math.
items.caption: $6 a day is about $182 a month. Invested 30 years at 7%: ~$223K. Sounds bad. Now find an apartment $300/month cheaper: same 30 years, ~$366K. One decision, made once, beats 10,950 skipped lattes. Order the coffee. Look at your rent. (7%/yr average assumed; illustrative, not advice.)

items.title: Fifty years, and no one has found him. Let me tell you how I did it.
items.caption: The Cask of Amontillado (Edgar Allan Poe, 1846), told by Montresor. He insulted me. So I invited him down to my vaults for a rare wine... and brought stones and mortar. 🕯️ He's chained. What happens next? 🎧 Sound on for the bells.

items.title: Your 2% cash back vs. a 20% APR
items.caption: Black Friday: $1,000 on a 2% cash-back card = $20 back. Pay only the minimum and ~20% APR (Bankrate's average) costs about $17 a month on that $1,000. Two months in, you've paid ~$33 for a $20 reward. Cash back only works if you pay in full, every month. (Simplified; not advice.)

items.title: 0% financing or $3,000 cash back? Depends on one number.
items.caption: $30,000 car, 60 months. Offer 1: 0% APR = $500/mo, $30,000 total. Offer 2: $3,000 back and finance $27,000 yourself. At 6.5% that's $528/mo, $31,697 total: 0% wins. At 4%: $29,835: the rebate wins. The break-even is about 4.2%. Get your own rate before you sit down. (Excludes taxes/fees; not advice.)

items.title: Half my kingdom is dead. So I locked the gates, and threw a party.
items.caption: The Masque of the Red Death (Edgar Allan Poe, 1842), told by Prince Prospero. Seven rooms, seven colors. An ebony clock that stops the music every hour. And at midnight, a guest no one invited. 🕯️ What would you have done?

items.title: Your $1,200 car repair, paid with minimum payments, costs $2,333
items.caption: Car won't start. $1,200 repair, $214 in checking. It goes on a 22% card and you pay the ~$34 minimum: 7 years 4 months and $1,133 in interest. Rewind: $100/month into savings for one year = the same repair, paid in cash, $0 interest. An emergency fund isn't to get rich. It stops emergencies from getting expensive. (Minimums vary by issuer; illustrative, not advice.)
